extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent applicants, judges, and intellectual property lawyers
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a patent specification satisfies the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. §112(a) — i.e., whether the disclosure enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory enablement requirement (§112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must include "a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art . . . to make and use the [invention]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline statutory command. Evaluation asks whether the disclosure enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention as claimed. The Court enforces the statutory language as written and reviews lower-court judgments accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-of-claims vs specification (claims measure the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent claims an entire class of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class; the claims measure the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The broader the claim, the more the specification must enable. Courts compare the full scope of the asserted claims to the enabling disclosure. Precedents: Morse, Incandescent Lamp, Holland Furniture, Continental Paper Bag Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement proportional to claim breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The more one claims, the more one must enable — a party seeking a broader monopoly must provide broader enabling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is not a fixed quantity; it scales with claim breadth. A patentee cannot claim 'sovereignty over [an] entire kingdom' without enabling that kingdom. This principle applies irrespective of technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible reasonable experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation to make and use a patented invention; what is "reasonable" depends on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior cases (Wood, Minerals Separation, Mowry v. Whitney, Tilghman v. Proctor) show courts tolerate some testing or adaptation by skilled artisans. But tolerance is limited: experimentation must be reasonable, not 'painstaking' or tantamount to discovery by trial-and-error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples plus disclosure of a common quality can suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification need not describe every embodiment if it gives one or a few examples and also discloses 'some general quality . . . running through' the claimed class that imparts a 'peculiar fitness' for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the inventor identifies a general, enabling characteristic common to the claimed class, examples together with that disclosed quality can enable the full genus (illustrated by Incandescent Lamp). The specification should reveal how to select or recognize embodiments based on that common quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claiming requires disclosure of enabling attributes (avoid pure functional drafting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define a genus by function (what the thing does) still must be supported by disclosure showing how to make and use the full range of embodiments; mere functional description of inputs or components is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing a key input or element only by its 'use or function' rather than its physical or chemical properties can render a claim non-enabled if it forces others to engage in 'elaborate experimentation' to find workable embodiments (see Holland Furniture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere roadmaps or directions to perform research are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction that amounts to a 'roadmap' (describe the inventor's trial-and-error process) or 'conservative substitution' (make substitutions and test) does not enable a claimed genus when it leaves practitioners to engage in random or extensive trial-and-error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the disclosed methods amount to research assignments or invite 'painstaking experimentation' or a 'hunting license,' they fail enablement. The Court treated Amgen's 'roadmap' and 'conservative substitution' as illustrative anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement judged from perspective of person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The adequacy of disclosure is measured by whether 'any person skilled in the art' could make and use the invention, given the specification and the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony, the predictability/unpredictability of the field, and the state of scientific knowledge bear on enablement. Unpredictable arts (e.g., antibody structure-function relationships) may make broad enabling disclosure harder to meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must disclose manner and process of making and using
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond merely naming a class or function, the specification must describe 'the manner and process of making and using' the invention in adequate detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes identifying essential structural/chemical characteristics when necessary to enable reproduction. The Court emphasized that a bare statement of discovery without practical guidance is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public benefit / 'patent bargain' rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent law's disclosure requirements serve the quid-pro-quo: inventors receive limited exclusive rights in exchange for enabling the public to practice the invention after the patent term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement protects the public interest by ensuring adequate disclosure so the knowledge 'inures to the people' after expiration; courts enforce enablement to preserve this balance, per historical statutes and precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial and doctrinal constraints (no adding/subtracting statutory requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must apply the statutory enablement requirement as written and not impose requirements outside the statute nor ignore those within it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While applying precedent, judges should not effectively rewrite the statutory standard; at the same time, long-standing case law (Morse, Incandescent Lamp, Holland Furniture, etc.) informs the statute's application.
